1.	Was there an attempt to fight forest fire near Cold lake, Alberta, in Ootober, 1925?
2.	Were persons of the names of Martin and Shaw supposed to have taken part in fighting fire?
3.	Did they send in a bill for the work they were supposed to have done; if so, to what amount?
4.	Who is the fire marshal for the district around Cold lake?
5.	Did he make an investigation with regard to supposed fire? If so, how many witnesses did he call?
6.	What was the cost of calling said witnesses, and has a report been received by the government?

1.	A forest fire started on the north side
of Cold lake in the latter part of July and was effectively cut off and brought under control by August 8th. This fire apparently continued to smoulder inside the fire guards, and some time during September and October, two persons named Martin Nyhus and Lester Shaw, considered it advisable to make some extra fire guards. This was done without securing the authorization of the forest authorities.	,
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	Yes. Approximately $460.00 is claimed. Department is paying $88.00.
4.	The local Dominion fire ranger for the district around Cold lake is Mr. J. W. Allen.
5.	Yes. Four men who worked in the original fire. An investigation was also made by the district fire ranger at Edmonton.
6.	No expenditure was incurred in connection with witnesses, either by the local fire ranger or the district fire ranger. A report by the district fire ranger is on file.
Hon. GEORGE H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise) moved that the House go into committee to consider Bill No. 188 to amend the Excise Act.
Is it printed?

I am informed, Mr. Speaker, that the bill was printed and sent to the distribution office this morning. It was explained yesterday.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Removal of tobacco, etc.

Mr. Chairman, I think the object sought by my hon. friend is perfectly proper. As I understand it, the purpose of the bill is to enable trade to be carried on at ports where we have a customs warehouse, but no excise warehouse; that is, to enable Canadian goods to be sold in competition with American. This is quite right. It is a little dangerous, though; does my hon. friend think he has got everything safeguarded? I would have thought the easiest way would have been to make any customs bonded warehouse an excise bonded warehouse.

If every customs bonded
warehouse were made an excise bonded warehouse I am afraid the abuse would be still greater. It is understood that even* excise
Income War Tax Act

bonded warehouse in the country is subject to continual surveillance by an excise officer, and to the payment of a fee. It is pointed out that American cigarettes are brought in to these customs bonded warehouses and sold as ships stores to the fishermen going to the Grand Banks and elsewhere, without the payment of any duty and without the payment of any American excise. It is absolutely impossible for the Canadian manufacturers to compete with them, and the acting deputy minister of the department, who was also head of the excise branch, advises that the safest way would be to permit them to remove Canadian cigarettes of domestic manufacture from the excise bonded warehouse and place them in the customs bonded warehouse, where they would have no excise duty to pay. Section agreed to.
Section 2 agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.
INCOME WAR TAX ACT AMENDMENT Hon. George H. BOIVIN (Minister of Customs and Excise) moved the second reading of Bill No. 116, to amend the Income War Tax Act, 1917.

Motion agreed to, bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Duff in the chair.
On section 1-Gross revenue.

Paragraph (m) of this
section defines the gross revenue where a personal corporation has revenue from more than one source, in which case the gross revenue means the sum of the net profits from each source. Does this affect in any way what I think we will come to somewhere later in the bill, the subject matter of previous discussion, namely double taxation or taxation from two sources? I have not had time to consider this paragraph very carefully, and I was just wondering whether this definition will in any sense establish the principle of double taxation.

No, indeed. The definition just referred to is inserted for the express purpose of avoiding the possibility of double taxation. There is a clause further on in the bill which provides that all dividends upon which taxes have once been paid at their source, shall not again be taxable. My hon. friend will also see later on in the bill that a personal corporation is assimilated to a person, and therefore the dividends which may go through one, two or three holding companies will come to the final holding company or the personal corporation absolutely free from any except the original tax.
(Mr Hoivin]

What is the idea of confining that particular definition to personal corporations? It is rather badly drawn, but I take it that the intent of that paragraph is to confine it merely to personal corporations.
The gross revenue means the sum of the net profits from each source.

Is not that the
effect of the definition? The paragraph reads:
"Gross [DOT]revenue" (where a personal corporation has revenue from more than one source) means the sum of the net profits from each source.
I admit that the drafting is not what one would desire, but it seems to me the effect is that in the case of personal corporations having revenue from more than one source gross revenue shall mean the sum of the net profits from each source. Am I wrong?"

The sum of the' net profits from each source is right. The definition of gross revenue is required in the act and was not there before,, because that phrase is now used, in the section of the bill dealing with personal corporations; it will be found nowhere else. One of the requisites of a personal corporation is that its gross revenue must be, to the extent of one quarter or more, derived from the ownership of investments or from trading in investments. In all other cases the revenue taxed is the net revenue after exemption, but in order to determine whether or not the corporation is a personal corporation the gross revenue has to be considered. This is the only part in the 'bill where the words "gross revenue" are used.
I take it, then, that this refers only to personal corporations?
Yes.

When this resolution was in committee I suggested an amendment which would come properly under section 1. My suggestion was that a definition of the word "resident" be added. As I pointed out, certain gentlemen who live in Canada, possessing large incomes, go to Europe and England and say, "We do not live in Canada", and they pay no income tax here at all. When they go to England and France they say the same thing; they do not live there, but live in Canada. It seems that now there is one law for the rich and one law for the poor, and I ask the minister if he will not accept Bill No. 147, introduced by myself, and incorporate it in this present bill. It is too late now to advance my bill beyond the first reading, but I think the bill is a fair one. It is the law of

Income War Tax Act
the United States and of Australia. I do protest against the lopsided enforcement of the present act. I think the minister should look at Bill No. 147, and I am sure if he does, he will see that it is a perfectly fair bill. What are you going to say to the poor man who has to pay a tax of $40 or $60? I have heard of cases where men were summoned to the police court because they did not pay their income tax for smaller amounts than that, and the judge imposed a heavy fine on them for violating t'he act. I submit to the minister that this is the place to incorporate my amendment in the definition. I do not want to move an amendment and delay the committee, but I hope the minister will attend to this matter. A large number of wealthy people are evading payment of the income tax by saying that they do not live in Canada, although they are domiciled here, their business is here, they draw dividends from business carried on in Canada. I venture to say that the minister knows many of these cases himself, and I would like a statement of policy from him in that regard.

I have looked at Bill No. 147, which was introduced by my hon. friend a few days ago. The object of his bill is to prevent anyone from evading taxation, but while the persons he refers to may at the present time evade municipal taxation, owing to the fact that they are not in Canada at the time the municipal taxes are levied, I think I can pretty truthfully assure him that they do not evade federal taxation. The Income War Tax Act provides that:
There shall be assessed, levied and ipaid upon the income during the preceding year of every person,-
(i)	residing or ordinarily resident in Canada, or
(ii)	who remains in Canada during any calendar year for a period or periods equal to one hundred and eighty-three days, or
(iii)	who is employed in Canada, or
(iv)	who, not being a resident of Canada, is carrying on business in Canada, or
(v)	who, not being a resident of Canada, derives income for services rendered in Canada, to any person resident or carrying on business in Canada but only upon that portion of the income so earned by such non-resident.
We feel that this cannot be very well strengthened without causing hardship and without causing recrimination on the part of foreign countries. When it is provided that everyone who is ordinarily resident in Canada, everyone who resides in Canada, and everyone who remains in Canada during any calendar year for a period equal to 183 days, is obliged to pay income tax to the federal treasury, I really do not think it would be advisable to add the still more drastic terms of bill No. 147. In any event, if it was the
desire of the government to incorporate Bill No. 147 as part of this bill or as an amendment to it, it would be necessary for us to begin by introducing a new resolution, because it might entail a slight increase in taxation, and the government could only provide for that in the usual way by introducing a resolution in the committee of Ways and Means, having it adopted there, and a bill then submitted for the consideration of the House.
Mr. CHURiCH: I still think that something should be done in this connection, and I would like to have the minister say whether he will adopt my suggestion, yes or no. The minister knows that there are evasions of the income tax by wealth}^ people, and with all Tespect I do say that little or no effort, so far as I know, is being made to collect the tax from these people. We have had these people before the court of revision in Toronto, where they have claimed that they live in England, and have millions of dollars invested there. They claim the same thing in connection with the federal taxes. I would like the minister to say yes or no whether he will accept this amendment as set out in Bill No. 147.

As I pointed out before to
my hon. friend, the persons to whom he refers who evade the tax in Toronto pay their federal taxes to the federal government. They are unable to evade the federal tax with the excuse which was mentioned by my hon. friend, and the commissioner assures me that they are obliged to pay their federal taxes to the federal treasury, that they are reached by the present bill. As I pointed out to my hon. friend a moment ago, the adoption of his bill would necessitate a new resolution, and a long routine of procedure which would delay the adoption of the measure for several days.
Section 1 agreed to.
On section 2-Dividends to individuals to be liable to tax.

During the main discussion of the principle which is covered here, my hon. friend was asked whether he would not look after the case of people who are now being taxed on dividends for the first time this year in regard to their income of 1925. The income is pretty well spent by this time; they had no idea that they would be taxed, and I should like to know whether my hon. friend has come to the opinion that it is impossible to postpone that tax and make it applicable only to the income of 1926. My hon. friend will recollect that this point was stressed at some length, and I thought he was going to agree to the suggestion.
Income War Tax Act

Yes, I remember very well that the point was argued at some length, in two connections: first, the retroactive effect which it was proposed to give in the case of personal corporations going away back to the period of the inception of the corporation, and secondly, the taxing of the dividends earned by joint stock companies and distributed during the year 1925. Both matters were taken up and carefully discussed together, and submitted to the legal department of the Income Tax branch, and also to the Justice department. It was pointed out that the taxation of the dividends drawn in the year 1925 was perfectly within the rights of the Dominion government; in fact, it was pointed out that the retroactive effect in general would be legal and could be enforced. But I am leading up to the statement that it was deemed not to be advisable to give a general retroactive effect to the provisions of the present bill, but that in so far as the revenue earned during the year 1925 was concerned, it should not create any great hardship to the holders of these dividends to have to pay the taxes upon them, for the reason that in practically 90 per cent of the cases of taxpayers in the Dominion of Canada the taxes paid, even considering the taxes on the dividends, will be smaller this year than last year. That has been figured out and has been ascertained. There are a few individual cases where persons deriving almost their entire income from dividends will have to pay slightly more taxation this year than they did the year before, but it was pointed out that the changes in the income tax law are always made at the time of the budget, that in so far as last year is concerned these people should have made provision for any possible change in the income tax so brought down, that it has been customary to make these changes when the budget is introduced and to make them apply to the previous year, and that no serious hardship would be felt, providing, however, that the retroactive effect would not extend further than one year, and that is the year upon which the taxes are being paid. In deference to the wish expressed by the hon. member for West York, the former Minister of Finance I propose later on to introduce a clause removing the drastic retroactive effect from the personal corporation dividends.
In the amendment which the minister proposes to introduce will the 1925 dividends of corporations be taxed on the same basis as they were last year?

No, the dividends from
corporations will be taxed upon the new basis-that is to say the earnings of corporations will be taxed at 9 per cent instead of 10J. The dividends derived from corporations and taxed as income to the shareholders will be taxed, of course, under the new schedule of rates. In other words the entire bill, with its advantages and disadvantages, will be applicable to the revenue earned during the year 1925.

-Will the minister state
whether he considers it would be within the powers of parliament not only to enact legislation for the purpose but to collect taxes on income earned, say ten years ago?

There is nothing which
would prevent the government, if it so desired and parliament approved, from reaching back for ten years and collecting taxes on income earned at that time. But we do not propose to do that. We propose only to collect the new tax on the dividends earned last year, on the dividends for which return was not made at the time the new bill was in-, troduced, on the dividends earned during the year which was dealt with by the Minister of Finance when the budget was introduced into the House. We propose to follow the custom which has always been followed in the administration of the Income Tax Act, that it be made applicable to the returns filed during the year in which the income tax changes were made.

In other words the minister states that income from dividends earned ten years ago would be on the same. basis as incomes from dividends paid in 1925 in so far as the legal powers of enacting legislation and collecting taxes thereon are concerned.

If my hon. friend will look at the book, the very excellent book written by Mr. Lefroy on The Canadian Federal System, he will find that Mr. Lefroy states:
There is nothing whatever to prevent the parliament of Canada, or even the provincial legislatures, from legislating retrospectively in relatioai to all matters within their respective jurisdictions.
I do not mean to say that to go back ten years would be a good principle. As I have just stated to the hon. member for West York we have considered the representations made, and we have decided that there will be no retroactive effect to our legislation previous to the year which is now being budgeted

Income War Tax Act
upon and for which the returns were made after the changes were introduced in this House.

Is the quotation which my
hon. friend has just read the basis of the opinion given by the Department of Justice and the legal officers in the Income Tax branch?
I did not ask all the officers of both departments what books they had read before giving their opinion.

I am asking is that the
basis of the opinion?

It would form a very good
basis for the conclusion I would arrive at, that our legislation is legal , but I understand there are many other authorities, that in fact the Income War Tax Act itself was amended in the same way by a previous government some time ago. Originally, if the tax was not collected within three years it became prescribed. It was found that a great many abuses occurred under this provision, and very rightly my hon. friends now sitting opposite introduced an amendment giving the tax retroactive effect, claiming that all income taxation not paid to the Dominion government should be paid and should be collected. Under that retroactive effect many amounts were made payable which had become prescribed under the former law. The matter has been tested in the courts and my hon. friends were found to be absolutely right. It was decided that the parliament of Canada had the power in. question.

I think my hon. friend has missed the point. I argued the point at some length the last day this matter was before us, and I enunciated the principle my hon. friend has quoted from Lefroy, namely, that it is within the competence of parliament to enact such legislation-there is no argument about that. But this is a tax against the income of the individual; it is a tax against property and being a tax against property, it must attach to the property. My point is, however, that if the property has ceased to exist there is nothing for the tax to attach to; and as the Minister of Customs admits, the property is just in the same position, whether it was earned ten years ago or last year, insofar as the collection of taxes is concerned. The income earned ten years ago forms, perhaps, a better basis for a picture. The income which was earned ten years ago is indisputably out of existence, and so is the income that was earned last year. That property has ceased to exist. Therefore, though parliament may
pass an enactment taxing the income that was earned in any year, the power of collection does not exist because there is nothing for the tax to attach to. It must attach against something, but it being a tax against property there is nothing for it to attach to because the property does not exist. That is where I submit the minister is wrong and where; if he has quoted the whole opinion of the Department of Justice and the legal advisers of the Income Tax branch, they are wrong. I suggest that the full details of their opinions be given to parliament because if they base them upon the quotation from Lefroy undoubtedly their position is sound- that is that parliament has the power to pass the legislation. But I say there is no power to collect a tax against property because there is nothing for the tax to attach to, the property having ceased to exist.

Well, if my hon. friend was right, there would be hundreds of people in Canada who would pay no income tax, and I for one would have paid none during three years, because at the time I came to make up my income tax returns I found the money upon which I was paying my income tax had ceased to exist-

That is not the point.
Mr. BOIVlN: -and I was obliged to borrow in order to pay it. That would apply absolutely to the argument of my hon. friend who says that the dividends earned during 1925 have ceased to exist. Is that the argument he makes?

May I put the matter in this way: Take last year when there was no amendment before the House. The Minister of Customs knew the year previous-the year that he was earning his income-exactly what taxes he had to pay. As he earned income the tax attached to it,' and he was bound by law to set aside a sufficient portion to meet that tax. And so in regard to the ordinary income earned last year: In so far as our taxation was not increased and made retroactive we all knew what tax was going to attach to it and we were bound to make the necessary provision to meet it. If the minister was foolish enough to spend the money, to make no provision for taxation, and to be under the necessity of borrowing, that was a matter of business and he' was a poor business man. He was bound to set aside something to meet the tax. The taxpayer did not know last year, when he was earning his income, and setting aside something, that the government would this year increase the tax to be paid upon last year's income. If he had known
Income War Tax Act

that legislation was to be passed, it might have been different. He did not know, did not make provision and thought he was entitled to spend every cent of his income, except that portion necessary to provide for the taxes which were then applicable to his income. The situation to-day is therefore quite different from that which my hon. friend has described as the one which influenced him in his decision to spend all his income.

I am surprised the hon. gentlemen is getting so scrupulous about the retroactive effect of this measure. Under the old act, as I pointed out recently before doming to this House, the people who were married, having a community of property, were taxed as having one single income; in fact, they had only one margin of exemption, but people who had not a community of property had two margins. But in 19X6 there was a dpubt. People married under the regime of community of property-and I was one of them-made their return under two separate forms, one-half of the income being attributed to the husband and one-half to the wife. The department refused to accept these returns. Tftey claimed the taxation should be levied on one income, and therefore there would be only one margin of exemption. I got an opinion from one of the most eminent civil lawyers' in Montreal and sent it to the department. The Minister of Justice had the law amended and made retroactive, so as to force us to pay for the year 1916 and the year 1917 with one margin of exemption, while other people were allowed two margins of exemption. That was a clear case of injustice, as pointed out by the hon. member who has resumed his seat, but I do not see that there were any scruples of conscience on the part of any Tory members, because that principle was applied for six years against all married people having community of property. In my case, I had only one margin of exemption while married people having separate property had two margins.
Did any one contest it?
I protested it.

But the hon. member did
not contest it in court?

No, I was not going to
spend any more money, but I was in the same position as my hon. friend, relying upon the law, upon the principle of justice, and upon the legal opinion which I had obtained with reference to taxation based upon equity and common sense, and upon what I under-

stood was the law. But the Justice department interpreted it otherwise, got parliament to sanction that interpretation and enacted it into law.

That is the point the Minister of Customs referred to-that parliament had passed the law. Undoubtedly parliament has passed lots of legislation which, if certain aspects of it had been contested in the courts, might have been found to be ineffective. If my hon. friend had contested the case in the courts, it might have been found that he was not liable to pay the retroactive tax, especially if it were on property which ceased to exist.

When the resolution preliminary to the bill was introduced, I urged somewhat strenuously that the dividend income of the tax-payer for the year 1925 should not be increased by ex post facto legislation. The hon. member for Labelle has pointed out a case of ex post facto legislation which certainly did cause a very great deal of irritation in the province of Quebec, to which it alone applied. But the fact that the department insisted upon clearing up the doubt in regard to the meaning of the act by subsequent legislation which became retroactive, is no reason in my opinion why this parliament should now create similar grievances. I quite understand that nn the majority lof cases, as the Minister of 'Customs has suggested, this provision will decrease the tax payable by individual holders of stock in Canadian companies. But there is a great number of cases where they will suffer grievances. I have to accept what the minister says, that the increased tax will apply to only ten per cent of the tax-payers, but I know a number of people who have suffered grievances. I know of cases where, if this provision applies to 1925, they will pay two or three times as much and they are not people with large incomes either. I pointed out to the hon. member the other day a case which came under my notice-I have the correspondence in my desk-of a clergyman who is retiring, and whose entire savings of a lifetime are invested in stock of Canadian companies. Under this act he will be compelled to pay nearly three times the amount he would have paid upon his income in 1924. The number of such cases may be ten per cent. That would mean that nearly two thousand people will undoubtedly pay more for 1925 under this legislation than they would have paid under the legislation existing up till April. That will cause -very serious grievances, and I think these people are justified in complaining. It is imposing upon them a burden which they should not

Income War Tax Act
have to bear, and I take issue with the government on that point. Any man having a small investment in Canadian companies up to December 1925 could not foresee that parliament was going to increase his taxation two or three times by legislation introduced in April 1926. That is a grievance which should not be allowed to exist. It will cause great irritation and dissatisfaction, and therefore I suggest that the best way to proceed is this: In so far as the income tax payable for 1925 is concerned, no tax-payer should be compelled to pay more than he would have paid under the legislation existing up to April 1926. That would be fair. If you wish to make a reduction to others, well and good, but do not increase the tax on one or two thousand people who, to my mind, are largely people whose incomes depend upon estates which are being administered by trust companies and trustees. I am not referring to the widow and orphan class. Do not make those people pay two or three times as much as they would otherwise have paid in order to make .up the deficiency in income due to the reduction of the taxation of other people with respect to 1925. With regard to 1926 they can get rid of their stock, sell it for what it is worth, and invest it in other things. I am suggesting to the minister that a fair way is to have a proviso that by reason of this legislation people should not be compelled to paj' now with regard to 1925 incomes more than they would have paid under legislation existing during 1925.
Mr. 'BENNETT:	I should like to add a
few arguments to those advanced by my hon. friend with respect to the desirability of removing this difficulty if possible. In a recent issue of the Free Press there was an editorial on double taxation pointing out that the minister had been making a very earnest effort to meet the difficulties of the situation as they were apparent to him and also expressing the hope that he might meet them. This is a real, not an imaginary grievance; it is double taxation in the very worst sense. The effect of it is to induce Canadian holders of securities of their own country to sell them and to invest the money in United States securities. Prior to the enactment of this legislation it is perfectly clear that there was a direct inducement to a man having money to invest it in Canadian enterprises because the dividends he received from it were free from normal tax. As the legislation now stands there is no freedom from normal tax on the part of those dividends and dividends which he receives from a United States investment stand on exactly the same basis as
dividends which he receives from a Canadian investment. I think the minister admitted that the other evening. The discrimination is therefore only against Canadian investments.
I suggest in addition to what the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Cahan) has suggested, that in respect to dividends of 1925 the law is obviously unfair for this reason. Brokers and bond sellers, have been disposing of securities and advertising in the public press during 1925 that income from preferred shares, for instance, of their companies would be free from normal tax, and stating what the normal tax was. It is clear that as the legislation now stands there is no freedom from normal tax, but the income from those dividends on Canadian securities is to be taxed just as incomes from dividends on Canadian securities were taxed before this law came into operation.
I will give an illustration from my own experience. I have some preferred shares, we will say for the sake of argument, in a Canadian company and last year let us say that I received $5,000 in dividends. That $5,000 in dividends having in the hands of the company paid tax once to the government, came into my hands free from normal lax. When my tax return was made out I received the benefit of the tax paid by the corporation on that money. There was therefore freedom from normal tax. Let me say also for the sake of argument that I had some shares in the American Telephone and Telegraph Company from which I received $1,000. That $1,000 in dividends in my hands paid income tax upon the whole amount because, as this was a foreign corporation, there was no freedom from normal tax. That is, this country's exchequer had received no money from the corporate income of that company. The effect of this legislation is to place my Canadian securities upon exactly the same basis as my United States securities. I can see no answer to that as regards the tax returns. I observe it has been suggested that such is not the case, but the evidence is that the dividends of $5b000 which I received from the Canadian company in 1925 are going to be taxed at exactly the same rate as the money which I received from the United States company. I have to put them into my tax returns as moneys received from that Canadian company, upon which money I pay that rate. It is true that the United States corporate tax is a higher tax than the Canadian corporate tax, but the money as it comes into my hands pays the same form of taxation in both instances.
Income War Tax Act

When for instance people of small means whom I know bought some preferred shares last year it was said in the literature on the subject that those shares were free from normal tax and these people bought on the strength of the legislation then existing with reference to 1925. It appears to me that the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is only fair when he asks that parliament should declare in a section attached to this legislation that nothing therein contained should be taken as compelling payment by the taxpayer of a higher tax in 1926 than he would have paid under the act that was in force in 1925 on the income derived by him from the very sources that paid it.
The minister should go a step further. I think the other evening he admitted the difficulty of double taxation. It is not only double but treble taxation in some instances and I will give an illustration that has come under my observation. The directors of a Canadian company gave dividends to a trust company that was appointed executor of a man's estate. In the hands of the trust company the department insisted upon payment of income tax upon that money as income derived from the estate of the testator.
3 p.m. Then the trust company distributed that money to the several persons named and in their hands the department also sought income tax on that money. I know that a. protest was made at the time the tax was paid but I know that the given sum of money, say "X", paid taxes three times before it reached the ultimate beneficiary. That is a fact. Whether it is right or wrong I do not know. The protest which was made at the time was unavailing and the tax was paid, "X" money paid tax, first, as owing by the corporation that earned it; second, in the hands of the trust company that received it for distribution and, third, in the hands of the ultimate beneficiaries to whom it was paid by the trust company. I can give the names and the amounts if necessary. Those are facts. In every instance, however, there was a freedom from normal tax on money in the hands of trust companies that received dividends in the manner I have indicated and in the hands of the ultimate beneficiaries. The minister realizes the difficulty and if he is not able to make what is suggested of universal application, he should make it of limited application at any rate for the smaller taxpayer. It seems to me that is desirable.

The minister said the other evening that they were considering the matter. The journal to which I referred in its editorial hoped that he might be able to find some solution. I suggest as a solution that we should add to the bill a section declaring that with respect to Canadian dividends there should be a reduction of say 4 per cent from the tax; that is that all Canadian dividends should be free from a normal tax of say 4 per cent. That would give an incentive to Canadians to invest their money in Canadian enterprises rather than send it to the United States. I know whereof I speak when I say that since this budget came down, there has been a realization to no inconsiderable extent of Canadian securities and the money has been invested in United States securities, first, because their market ability is greater than ours and, second, because the return is larger than ours. I know a gentleman who tells me that he always invests his money in United States securities because he gets larger returns. "Now," he said, "it is settled, I would not care to put them in Canadian securities at all because I get no allowance for my normal tax. I pay my corporation tax, and then I pay the full tax, the same as I would in the United States; and I can realize upon my securities much more quickly and get a better return in the United States than here." If anything can be done to meet this situation of double taxation, however slight it might be, I am sure it would serve as an incentive to people to invest their money in enterprises in this country. As it now stands, any man with 810,000 to invest will not feel disposed to put that money into enterprises in Canada, knowing that by so doing he will have to pay 9 per cent on any money that is earned in the hands of a corporation, and then the full tax, without any allowance for normal tax, on the income as it is paid to him by way of dividends. If the minister can effect that purpose I think he will be doing Canadian industry some service, and he will be giving some slight inducement to Canadians to invest their money in Canadian enterprises rather than in those of a foreign country. Those are the suggestions I desire to make to the minister.

On section 3, subsection (11)-Carrying charges.

In what degree does this differ from the corresponding paragraph of the resolution, No. 8 I believe? Under this paragraph people holding property, some parts productive and other parts unproductive, heretofore were allowed, quite properly, to deduct from the income of their productive property the taxes paid or losses incurred upon their unproductive property. The member for Port William (Mr. Manion) and several other hon. gentlemen raised the point, and the minister made it quite clear, I think, that it was his intention to cover it. He said he wanted to reach the speculator who was investing some of his surplus income in real estate for speculative purposes and thus evading taxation. The other point is this. I know many instances, for example, of a family holding a couple of houses or tenements which are returning an income, and holding besides two or three vacant lots as part of the estate. Very often the latter class of property cannot be readily sold for what it is worth. It is not held for speculative purposes, but municipal taxes are levied upon it every year. Surely it is as equitable that the owners should be allowed to deduct the losses upon the unproductive property from the income returned by their productive property as it is for a company before distributing dividends to deduct losses incurred and taxation paid upon unproductive property. I understand that companies are covered. It is said that:
The carrying charges or expenses of unproductive property or assets not acquired for the purposes of a trade, business or calling, or of a liability not incurred in connection with a trade, business or calling, dhall not be allowed as a deduction in determining income for the year 1925 and each year thereafter.
The result is that the speculator who trades in real estate will under this clause be able to deduct the taxes he pays on unproductive property from the income he receives on productive property; but the small property-owner, one of the most useful type of ratepayers and citizens, will be unjustly treated.

I think it is unsound legislation. It could be covered without much change in the tax law, provided of' course it was interpreted in the proper spirit.

This subsection is nothing more than an amplification of subsection 8 of section 3 of the act, which reads as follows:
In computing the amount of the profits or gains to be assessed ,a deduction shall not be allowed in respect of disbursements or expenses no-t wholly, exclusively and necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income.
As to income from the taxpayer's chief occupation, the subsection proposed is to render certain what has been deemed to be the law heretofore, namely, that the profits of a person derived from a trade, business or calling, if invested in unproductive property not required for the carrying on of the business, precludes the carrying charges of that property from being allowed as a deduction from the annual revenue of the particular business or calling. Such expenses are not necessarily laid out or expended for the purpose of earning the income, but rather for the carrying of a capital non-productive asset.
As to income from sources other than the chief trade, business or calling, that has generally been termed a secondary income. It may be said by way of example that taxes and interest in respect of unproductive real estate would not be allowed as against say, income from royalties. However, the interest payable in respect of the money borrowed, of which the unproductive property represents the security, may be set against the interest received on money loaned by the taxpayer but taxes, local improvements, assessments and like carrying charges of unproductive real estate are not proper deductions against income derived from salary or from interest. Such charges naturally should be capitalized; they should be added to the cost of the property in order to determine whether or not a profit is made at the time the property is sold, which profit, of course, is now exempt from taxation. The main point is that the expenditure is not made in the earning of income; it is an expenditure on capital account, and expenditures in connection with capital do not come within the purview of the income tax act. Notwithstanding what may be said to the contrary, the clause in its present form appears to me absolutely fair and logical, because all that a taxpayer is entitled to deduct in computing his income should be expenditures made to earn the income or in the hope of earning it. The carry-14011-275	.

The income tax act is not and cannot always be in every respect strictly logical; in some cases it may not always be absolutely fair, but so far as this clause is concerned, if fairness and logic are to be appealed to, all I have to say is that it is pretty difficult to find words in which to enact a clause which might be fairer. If he is not ,a dealer in real estate, or if he is an investor and has a certain number of tenements or houses which he rents, the carrying charges of all his real estate will certainly be liable as a charge against the revenue derived from part of the real estate. But I do not see how a clause could be worded to get over the difficulty presented by the hon. member for Labelle if at the same time we do not exempt all real estate which is unproductive and which is being held as an investment. After all, no matter what may be the value of a property, it is undoubtedly held in the hope of a future sale and profit. "Hope springs eternal in the human breast.'' I am willing to admit that in a great many cases the hopes are never realized, and that in a great many cases the property is eventually sold at a loss. But perhaps it would have been better if the property had been sold years previously; perhaps the loss might not have been so great, and the carrying charges would have been saved. There is no doubt that when property is held it is held in the hope of an eventual profit, and that profit must include the taxes paid on the property. The income tax act does not touch that profit; it is left clear in the hands

With reference to section 4 (1A), I must again appeal to the minister to consider the question of the exemption of children. We have heard on many occasions during the budget debate, and again in this debate, of the interests of corporations and the advantage of inducing people to invest in industrial pursuits; but I repeat now what I stated on a previous occasion, that the great defect of the fiscal legislation of almost all countries is to forget the state of the family, is to forget that the primary advantage of a country is the establishment of a family, and that the duty of the state is to alleviate as much as possible the burdens of fathers and mothers. Why adopt the age of eighteen instead of twenty-one? Twenty-one is the legal age. Until a child has reached the age of twenty-one he is under the legal and social responsibility of his father and mother. Even in the English provinces, and under some legislation of our province which is not in harmony with our church legislation, marriages between two minor children, both of marriageable age, are declared null if not ac-

Income War Tax Act
companied by the consent of their parents. Therefore, until they have reached the age of twenty-one, boys and girls are not full-fledged citizens and ratepayers; they have not complete liberty of action. Besides, under the previous law, as under this law, there is ample margin for the government to do away with the exemption in case of children earning their own living. The section itself says:
For each child under eighteen years of age who is dependent upon the taxpayer for support.
Why should you tax the parents who have in their charge boys and girls of nineteen, twenty, and twenty-one years of age? That is the very time of life when their maintenance and education is the most expensive to the parents. It seems to me it is precisely at that period of family life that the parents should be helped and considered by the state. Therefore I again appeal to the government -we shall have to do it one day or another, because public opinion will force it upon us-why not be agreeable to it now and raise the margin of exemption from eighteen to twenty-one years of age? If it is said that a large number of children between eighteen and twenty-one years of age are earning their living, then I repeat you have under this clause, as well as under the preceding law, power to prevent parents claiming exemption on account of children who are earning their livelihood. Even at the present time there are children of sixteen and seventeen years of age whose parents cannot claim exemption for them under the present law. Therefore this only applies, I repeat, to those parents who have the will and the courage to impose upon themselves the necessary sacrifices to give further education to their children, who endeavour to make of their children more useful citizens, and try to arm them for the battle of life as well as for the responsibilities of citizenship. I think they should be encouraged. We read much about the advantages of education, but when the father and mother impose upon themselves sacrifices to give a better education to their children, the state steps in and says: You shall pay the penalty of your devotion to your child, to the state, and to society. It is all wrong; it is inspired by a false conception of the duty of the state towards the family. Means could easily be found to recoup the state for the little difference this would mean in the taxation raised.
I think this matter should be considered right now, when we are speaking of reducing the burdens of the people of this country, when we are speaking of inducing people to be more hopeful of the future of this country.
If there is a class of people that demand the sympathy of the state and of parliament, it is those men and women who have the courage to establish a family and to impose upon themselves sacrifices in order to make of their children as useful and as cultured citizens as they can possibly become. It seems to me there should be no hesitation, Mr. Chairman, in making the age of exemption coincident with what has been adopted in all our civil laws as the age of full maturity, of full emancipation for the children. Up to the age of twenty-one they are socially, morally and legally a charge upon their parents to a greater or to a lesser degree; the principle is there, and I think the principle should carry here. Until the civil codes of the various provinces are amended so as to say that children are fully emancipated at eighteen years of age, I do not see why you should tax parents for the maintenance and education of their children between the age of eighteen and the full age of civil emancipation, which is twenty-one. If I can find a seconder I would move that the words "twenty-one" be substituted for the word "eighteen."

It is for the good of the state in every way that that should be done, and if the children are given a proper education, it means that the father has to keep on supporting them until they are twenty-one years of age or thereabouts. But the poor individual who has eight or ten children to raise, who is not allowed the amount of rental he pays on his house if he owns none, who is not allowed the taxes he may pay on a small piece of property he is keeping as a legacy for some of his children, is looked after very carefully and keenly by the officials of the department. He is easily reached, first, because he is honest and, second, because the value of his property and goods is readily determined by the taxing bodies of the government, whereas the large capitalist or investor, about whom so many hon. gentlemen have spoken with such tenderness, is the one who finds the greatest ease in evading taxation.
The minister cannot devise any form of taxation to cover all forms of fraud perpetrated oit the treasury. No minister, no department, will ever be able to do that, but that should not distract us from the social aspect of a fiscal system, of taxation and of government. I repeat, in a country like ours where we are crying out for population, where we are spending millions to attract foreigners to build up Canada, can we not make a little sacrifice to help the people born and brought up in this country who are trying to increase our population by the most natural law, by the law that has been made and blessed by God, but which unfortunately is being evaded by an increasing number of taxpayers?

A company which by its letters patent or supplementary letters patent,-

In support of
what my hon. friend has said I would point out that in Ontario I know of trading concerns which, for the purpose of ease in carrying on business, have been incorporated. Although the stock is distributed the payments out of profits are not distributed on a stock basis. They meet together and apportion the profits in accordance with the activities of the different members during the year; sometimes one will get more and sometimes the other, although the holdings are exactly the same. We have a number of companies of that kind, and I really think they should have this option, if the minister can see his way clear to adopt it.

I agree with what has been
6aid by both hon. gentlemen; I think these companies should not be treated as a corporation if they desire to be considered a partnership. -a corporation. . . . eighty per centum of the stock of which is owned by persons actively employed in the business of the corporation or by such persons and their families.

He brings these people into the business; he wants their continued interest, support and assistance. It is not necessary that they should be relatives, nor is it necessary that they should be members of the same family so long as they have an interest and are actively engaged in the business. Would the minister allo-w

ship. Also you must not get away from the idea that in all joint stock companies where the stock is not all held by the members of one family, or by former partners in the partnerships, then there enters into the administration of the company at least a different mode of accounting. Then salaries are paid to the directors of the company. Then the manager of the company is operating and administering property which belongs to somebody else. The director's are working both in their own interest as shareholders, and also to earn their salaries as directors of the company.

Why not make it 60 per

I would be disposed to

It would only increase it

I would obviate that by

I do not think that allowing three or four old employees to go to their neighbours and secure assistance from them, they purchasing a minority share of the stock, would create any difficulty which could not be overcome very readily. If you wish to limit it, limit it as to the amount of capital. But as to these smaller companies, where you have men who are really in a partnership and some other person coming in with a limited partnership, it would apply in exactly the same way. They come in for the purpose of assisting local industry, and for the purpose of assisting temporarily those who are actively engaged in the business locally. I am sure if that were reduced, even if you reduce it to 60 per cent, it would give relief to such cases as I have in view because in all these cases the employees would own at least 60 per cent of the stock within a year or two.
I cannot follow that quite.

I need only add that
the answer of the government to any queries of this sort is useful only as indicating that the opposite to what the government informs the House is likely to take place. I cannot say I am surprised at what the government has done in proposing this amendment, nor is my state of mind affected one way or the other by the several assurances which came from various members of the government many times: first that amendments were not contemplated at all or intended, next that there would be none, and lastly, and in the most solemn possible form from the Minister of Finance, that there would be none that * would be substantial, and that if there were any they would just be a change in wording so as to make clear something about parts. All these assurances have gone the way of all assurances this government ever gave. They have proven to be wholly without any purpose, at least without any effect save to mislead the House, and to be wholly falsified by events. In a word they have been in every way worthy of the administration. Nor am I surprised at the character of the amendment itself. It is just about the kind that of retreat which one would expect this government to choose. One would never expect it to come out of the front door and admit it is wrong, but if there is any chance of escape 
out of the back door, under cover of an umbrella, that is the course the government will always pursue.
I am not at all out of sympathy with the object of the amendment; in fact its object is in line wholly with the central policy of the Conservative party, its historic policy. The government's course is merely a camouflage surrender to the principles which they have for many years denounced and to the men whom politically they have for many years derided. The way this should be done, as everybody knows, would be to restore the duty, pending investigation, to where it is placed by this amendment, at 26 per cent or slightly over, on lower priced automobiles, . and then remove the excise tax. Then, if anything be needed to further ensure a larger proportion of manufacture in Canada, it should be done in a straightforward way by the duties being further adjusted against importation of parts. This would be the frank and correct way, and the people would understand it, but it is just because the people would understand it that the government does not choose such a course-no other reason in the world. The excise tax is to be removed. All right, remove it in a straightforward way, and make what is left the duty. When you remove the excise tax on goods made in Canada and leave it on goods imported from the United States, then it is an excise no more; it is a duty. But the government want it called an excise in order that under such miserable camouflage they can can escape. That is the whole idea of this amendment. I would be delighted to support it if the government would reach the object in a frank, open way: put the duty at 26 per cent and remove the excise tax on automobiles under $1,200. Why is it not so done? Does any hon. gentleman suggest any other reason, save that they want to confuse the people of Canada? They want to secure by subterfuge and indirection what they have not the courage to secure by the open straight-forward way. What is to be thought of an administration which boasts of its hostility to protection-that is, boasts of it where they feel the cause is not strong and not popular, but is ready to secure all the protection possible as long as it is called "safeguarding;" an administration which is opposed to duties as such, but is ready to get duties as long as you call them "excise"? Such is the position of this government. And when they bring the amendment in they stand up and say: "Now we are ready to put this through, but if by any chance our precious political lives are imperilled we are ready to repeal or to withdraw it." If the

Special War Revenue Act
supine and spineless could go further than that, I have never witnessed it in my life.
Is there anything but the jelly-fish in the whole conduct of the administration on tariff matters? If this is essential, if this be the true mind of the government, why do they not come forward and declare it to be government policy and stand or fall by it, instead of holding it as a sword over the committee, saying, "If anybody opposes it we will drop it. It is right; we ought to do it, but it is not half as right as that we should be in power. It is valuable, but not half as valuable as our precious political lives." This is the attitude of the administration, and hon. members will not be deceived, and I hope the country will not be deceived, although certainly the government will endeavour to deceive it. This is merely the restoration of the duty to 26 per cent and the removal of the excise tax. That is all. The excise tax was not there for the purpose of raising the duty on automobiles. It was there to get revenue for Canada out of automobiles instead of having to get it out of what were considered more acute necessaries of life. If the government feel they can do without the revenue, well and good; let them do without the revenue; let them remove the excise. If they feel that the duty has to be reimposed in order to retain the industry in this Dominion, they will be supported by every member on this side of the House. They tell us that this is going to secure the manufacture of these goods in Canada. It is the duty that secures- the manufacture in Canada. If the manufacture consists more than it should of importation and assembly, then the frank, open way to remedy that situation is by a duty on the parts, thereby providing for manufacture of the parts in Canada.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), who is following me closely, knows this just as well as I; he knows that this is a camouflage; that it is intended to mislead and confuse the people of this country; that it is put in this form in order that ministers of the crown may go out and say: We reduced the tariff on automobiles to 20 per cent, when they did not do so. It is done in order that they may go out and say: We have cheapened them, and in order that they may pretend that they have cheapened them at the expense of the manufacturers when really they have cheapened them at the expense of the treasury of Canada, or in other words at the expense of the taxpayers of this Dominion.
All I rose to say was this:	When we have
a government taking a course and asking the
House to follow it, let that course be taken in the straightforward way, in the way the people will understand1. Do mot let it be t.aken in a circuitous way, by the subterfuge such as this, which leaves the law in such shape that we have a duty of 26 per cent, 6 per cent of it being called an excise tax when it is not an excise tax at all. In a word the government is calling a duty "excise" in order that, the people may not understand what is being done, the government thereby being relieved, so they hope, of the ignominy into which they have brought themselves.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I take direct
exception to my right hon. friend when he says that the government in this measure is proceeding in any indirect or circuitous way to attain an object which it has had in view with respect to all tariff changes which have been made during this sesion. The one object underlying the changes in the tariff this session has been to make commodities cheaper to the consumers of this country. The automobile is a necessity to practically all branches of industry and trade and to consumers in a large way; we have been endeavouring to make that particular commodity available at a lower rate to the consumer. We have Sought to do that first of all by a reduction in duty. We are seeking to take a step further in the same direction by the removal of a war tax hitherto imposed upon automobiles of $1,200 and under when manufactured in Canada. My hon. friend admits that that will be the effect of removing the excise at the present time. If that is the effect it is attaining the objedt this government has had in view ,in the tariff changes which have been introduced.
The customs duty on automobiles of $1,200 and under has been! cut 15 per cent. That cut remains 15 per cent and imy right hon. friend by no argument of any kind can refute that - statement. The tariff is there; it is printed so that everyone can read and make comparisons for himself, and the fiscal statement as it will appear after this budget has been adopted will disclose two facts, first, that the tariff on automobiles of $1,200 and under has been reduced 15 per cent, and that in addition on cars manufactured in Canada a 5 per cent war tax has been removed, which benefit the manufacturers of automobiles have undertaken to see is passed on to the consumers by way of an equivalent reduction in the price.
It has been stated that possibly the manufacturers will not keep their word in that particular. I for one am prepared to accept their word at the present time. But if it
Special War Revenue Act

is found that they do not keep their word in that particular, the government has at hand1 a remedy that can compel them to keep their word in a manner that will still further help the consumers of this country, and that is by removing the war tax on all cars of $1,200 and under, wherever manufactured. The government has power to do that by order in council without legislation because in this particular we can lower although we cannot raise taxation by order in council. If automobile manufacturers do not give to the consumers of this country the full benefit of the reduction in excise which we are making at the present time, this government by order in council will remove the 5 per cent excise on all oars of $1,200 and under. Having said that much, may I add this? My right hon. friend, I believe, desires to help the manufacturers of this country, but we on this side of the House are just as anxious as my hon. friend to help the manufacturers of this country. Hon. gentlemen opposite think the only way in which to help the manufacturing industry is by increasing tariffs, putting on more protection.

That is what this is
doing.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
To-night we
are showing by this method that we can help the manufacturers by taking off taxation. There is a great difference between imposing a tax to protect an industry and removing a tax in order by so doing to help consumers and incidentally to help manufacturers as well, as I believe and hope this will do in the case of the manufacturers of automobiles in Canada. If the removal of this excise tax tends to create a large demand for automobiles because of their selling at a lower rate it will certainly help that industry and ought to be beneficial to the automobile manufacturers. We believe it will have that effect. Just as we discovered that owing to the lower cost of agricultural implements the demand increased, so we believe with a lower cost of cars, the demand will increase.
My right hon. friend says a great deal at different times about manufacturing in Canada, about encouraging manufacture in this country. This is the removal of a tax affecting the product of Canadian industry. We are allowing the tax to remain on the product of United States industry; we are helping our own industry in this Dominion in a way which assists the consumer and the manufacturer at the same time. If an object 
of that kind is not laudable and worthy, I should like to know what object could be laudable and worthy. Again I repeat 9 p.m. that the change which the government is making at the present time is in the direction of the budget as introduced which aimed at removing taxation. The tariff has been reduced 15 per cent on automobiles of $1,200 and under. That reduction remains as it is, and now we are proposing this further removal on oars manufactured in Canada, of a 5 per cent tax which was imposed in time of war. May I add that to enjoy this immunity from taxation the cars manufactured must represent manufacture to the extent of at least 40 per cent for a year and 50 per cent thereafter in Canada, which means additional employment to and of labour in this country. That is another very important item. These are the objects which the government has had in view, and they are objects which should commend themselves to this House irrespective of party.
