The House in Committee on Bill No. 8 to amend the Canada Grain Act (warehouse receipts)-Mr. Campbell-Mr. Duff in the Chair.
On section 1

Contents of warehouse receipts.

The bill now before the House is to my mind of such importance, particularly to western Canada, that I feel I owe no apology to members of the House, coming as I do from the city of AVinnipeg, for taking the time necessary to discuss it and to explain its import.
Both sides of this House and all parties are one in their pride in respect to the position held by Canada to-day in the grain trade of the world. Canada stands in the very vanguard as an exporter of wheat, and to appreciate the importance of her position in that regard it is but necessary to state it. To-day the world wheat crop amounts to approximately three billion bushels. Much of the wheat is consumed by the countries producing it, and the number of wheat exporting countries is comparatively few. The amount of wheat required by importing countries over and above what they themselves produce is roughly seven hundred million bushels. Of this huge total Canada alone supplies about three hundred million bushels, or approximately half. Other countries together supply the balance; Argentina two hundred million bushels; United States one hundred million bushels; Australia ninety million bushels, with the remainder coming from the Danubian states, India and other small exporters.
It must be at once apparent to the House that in the building up of such a tremendous wheat export Canada must have developed machinery and handling equipment for that trade which represents a very considerable investment. In round figures the amount of private capital invested in plant and equipment for the handling of that export trade is

Canada Grain Act
186,000,000. This represents the investment by private companies in country elevators, terminal elevators and incidental equipment. Until at least three years ago the whole of this export trade was handled by what I may call private grain companies in close competition. The heart of the trade is Winnipeg, and its ramifications extend throughout the prairie provinces, their purpose being to gather the wheat crop of the prairie provinces and to convey it to terminal ports in order that thereby it may reach the markets of the world. Never has it been a monopoly. This trade has been carried on by companies entering into the keenest sort of competition.
Within recent years the movement in the west toward the co-operative marketing of grain has materialized and within the last three years there has appeared above the horizon in western Canada a new competitor. That new competitor is known in common parlance as the wheat pool. Let me remark here that so far as the wheat pool is concerned I as a western Canadian, I as a Canadian, cannot, nor do I, take any exception to the object it has set out to achieve. In so far as the purpose of the wheat pool is to gather and carry the produce of the western farmers to the markets of the world at as cheap a cost as possible, I am in entire accord therewith. The only question at issue, so far as this bill is concerned, is by what means shall it secure the object which it has set out to attain. It is this association known as the wheat pool that sponsors this bill No. 8. I shall refer to the grain trade, apart from the pool, in general terms as the grain trade. The grain trade oppose this bill because they see the effect of it is to imperil their investment by a means not available to the ordinary competitor, but by means of legislative enactment. When I say the grain trade takes exception, I am referring not to a trade that has been a discredit to this country, but to a trade that has been developed in this country throughout the many years that wheat has been produced and is generally recognized as being conducted in a very efficient manner.
The pool and the grain trade take issue on this amendment. This House is asked to decide between the two, and for that purpose I here and now wish to state the facts as I understand them after some investigation of the situation, and I hope I speak with some knowledge of it. I wish to state the facts merely as they are and leave to this House the matter of judgment. Before proceeding further it might be well to look for a moment at just what is the existing relationship between the producer of grain and the grain trade to which I am referring. Is the producer 14011-276
of grain to-day, without this amendment, at the mercy of the grain trade? Their relationship is regulated by the Canada Grain Act, administered by a Board of Grain Commissioners, a public body appointed by the government. Now comes the pool and asks that the Canada Grain Act be amended as set out in Bill No. 8. In order to appreciate the purpose of this amendment, as well as its effect generally on the grain trade in the west, it is necessary, chiefly for the benefit, if I may say so, of those members of the House who come from the east, to make just a brief survey of the method by Which the grain is collected on the western prairies and transmitted to the terminal ports whether they be at the head of the Great Lakes, Vancouver, Prince Rupert, or Duluth.
With a crop the size of the Canadian wheat crop, which last year was approximately 430,000,000 bushels, every member will at once appreciate the fact that it is necessary to establish warehouses where this grain may be stored, in two places: first, throughout the country, secondly, at the terminal points. If any member of this House desires to enter into the business of handling grain effectively, he must do this: he must establish terminal elevators at some terminal port, and he must also establish lines of elevators throughout the country to gather the grain in order that that grain may be fed into his terminal elevator. If any man entering the grain business invests his money in a terminal elevator without investing also in feeders throughout the country, there is only one end, and that is his terminal elevator will fail to get the grain from the country, and he must go out of business. Therefore he builds as feeders the country elevators, which collect the grain in competition with the elevators of competing companies, and having so collected the grain, their purpose is to carry that grain where? To the terminal elevator of his particular line. It is axiomatic, therefore, that if by any process of legislation or otherwise you commandeer the capacity of his country elevators, and having so commandeered it, take the grain that is stored in his country elevators and divert it from his terminal to the terminal of a competing company, you are thereby forcefully taking away business from his company, with what result? At first, loss of profit on his investment, and eventually, if carried to its logical conclusion, bankruptcy of his concern. If hon. members have followed that, I would like to say here, that just such 'an outcome is the tendency of this amendment. If I have money invested in a terminal elevator at Fort William, we will say, a ter-

Canada Grain Act

minall elevator of 1,000,000 bushels capacity, that will cost me approximately $1,000,000, and if I have a like amount or double or half the amount invested in country elevators acting as feeders to that terminal, then if by legislation you force my country elevators to feed, not my own terminal, but the terminal of a competitor you thereby do me injury. If that effect is brought about by oipen competition I can have no complaint. The grain trade in the west acknowledge that. They say that if their competitor, the pool, by virtue of ereteting terminal elevators at the points of export and by virtue of erecting or acquiring country elevators, secure a share of the grain trade and take it to their own terminal elevators, they accept that as being fair competition. But they do take exception to this House putting through the present bill which says in effect "you the private grain trade, with money invested in terminal facilities and in country elevator facilities, must accept into storage in your country elevators the grain of members of the wheat pool and not only that but at their direction, having so stored the grain in your country elevators, you must divert it from your terminals to their terminal which is the terminal of a 'competitor." I appeal to the fairness of this House, altogether 'apart from political expediency, I appeal to the business judgment of hon. members, to say if that is a sound business proposal?
Now, what reasons do the pool advance for the passing of legislation such as this? They state a principle and one which meets with popular approval; they state a principle to which I can take no exception. The wheat pool in western Canada is an association of producers of grain controlling to-day at least 50 per cent of the wheat of the west. Having so associated themselves for the purpose of marketing their own grain they say: We the growers of grain have the right to associate ourselves as a co-operative institution for the purpose of gathering our grain into warehouses or elevators in the country and storing it there until such time as we are ready to ship it, and having so stored it to maintain control over that identical grain and ship it from any elevator in which it may be in the west direct to the pool terminal. I accede at once to the soundness generally of the proposition that they have the right, as an association of wheat producers, to gather their grain, store it in country elevators, maintain the identity of that grain, maintain custody over it throughout, and ship it to their pool terminal. But the question arises at once how they are to effect

that purpose. Supposing the Minister of Agriculture, if I may take him as an example, decides that he will go into the business of handling, exporting and selling grain in the markets of the world, how would he proceed? I take it that he would have to proceed without any special legislation from this parliament. He would have to proceed in the way that every other private grain company in the west built up its trade. He would establish a plant of elevators both terminal and country, terminal elevators to store the grain which his country elevators would collect throughout the prairie provinces. How far would the Minister of Agriculture or any other private individual get if he or they acquired terminal elevator capacity at the head of the lakes, or at Vancouver, or at Duluth, and then said to me as a competing company or to any other private line company "I have capacity for the storage of grain at the head of the lakes, or at Duluth, or at Vancouver, or at Prince Rupert. Now I want grain to feed to my terminal elevator"? If he did that how far would he get? Would I, through my country elevators ship the grain I have collected to his terminal elevator? Would any other private operating company do so? No, not a bushel would he get. He would be bound, therefore, to enter into competition by a system of gathering elevators throughout the country, collecting the grain from the farmer, and then feeding his terminal. The grain trade say that the pool should proceed by the same method. But is it proceeding that way? Having first sold the idea of the pool to a considerable portion of the western farmers it binds them upon contract to do what? To deliver their grain to the pool. The question then arises: How shall this grain that is contracted by farmers to be delivered to the pool reach the pool terminals? The solution is along the lines of ordinary competition, and this would be the procedure: The pool, having decided to go into the grain handling' business, and having acquired terminal space at points of export, would then proceed to erect gathering elevators throughout the country, known as country elevators, and it would be through such elevators that it would feed its terminals. But so rapidly has the idea of the pool grown that it finds itself with more grain under contract than it has country elevator capacity .to handle. Therefore instead of at once proceeding to build sufficient country elevators to collect the grain from all pool farmers, it now seeks to take a short cut which is not the .line that can be taken by an ordinary competitor. And so it conceived, the idea

Canada Grain Act
that it would get legislation, passed so that it could say to the private line companies, "You must not only accept pool grain .for Storage at country points as you have to do at present under the act, but you must send it to such terminals as the pool farmer directs you to send it, not to your terminals at the ihead of the lakes, or at Vancouver, or at other points." Where will the pool farmer, under these circumstances, direct the private line companies to send the grain? The answer is obvious-to the pool terminal. Pool members will tell you frankly that is the purpose of this legislation. If you read it you will see that it gives the owner of grain the right to demand delivery in two places-either at the country point, where Stored, or on track in cars at the terminal .elevator which it sees fit to name, which is in fact the pool terminal elevator. I want hon. gentlemen to note this fact- because it is a matter of considerable importance, and I appeal to the fairminded-ness of those who have invested money in private enterprises-that if this bill goes through, a pool farmer can come to me, if I am the owner of a line of country elevators and terminals, bring in 1,500 bushels of wheat and say to me: "Store my wheat." I have to take it, as I do now under the law. He can come back in ten or fifteen days or two months, if the grain is still there, and say to me: "I want you to ship that grain to the pool terminal at Fort William." I would do that as the act now stands, provided he accepted delivery at that country point and took the chance of leakage and other hazards en route. But if this bill goes through, he can say to me: "I want you to deliver that grain not at your terminal but to the pool terminal, and you have to guarantee my weight and grain at the pool terminal." That is the situation. Under the existing act he can drive to my elevator in the country and say to me: "What grade will you give me for this grain?" I say: "No. 2 northern, a certain per cent dockage." If he in his experience and judgment considers that that is the proper grade and proper dockage, he will say: "Agreed; take it in store." I have got to take it in store. As the law now stands I am responsible for the safe keeping of that grain. I give him a warehouse receipt which certifies that I have received into store at that country point 1,500 bushels of No. 2 northern wheat, with a certain dockage. I must keep that in store; but if I need extra space in my elevator I have the right, upon giving him forty-eight hours' notice, to ship that wheat to some 14011-2761
terminal point; or he himself can come in at any time the grain is in storage and, having ordered a car, order it loaded. According to the practice of the grain trade at present, when I ship it from my country point to my own terminal elevator I guarantee to him at the terminal point grade and weight. That is as the law now stands. Having received into store at the country point 1,500 bushels of No. 2 northern, I must deliver to him at my terminal elevator at any terminal point he may name a warehouse receipt calling for the same weight and grade of grain. But mark you, under the existing law I can afford to do that. I can afford to guarantee him weight and grade at the terminal point, because not only have I got the handling charges of that grain at the country point, which are fixed by law, but having transmitted it to my terminal I have there the benefit of the additional charges for handling and storage. There is no member of the pool but will acknowledge that the profitable end of the grain business is at the terminal elevator. That is the most lucrative part of the business.
Hear, hear.

I observe
that hon. members agree. Now if by legislation you divert the grain from my country elevators to the terminal of the pool, which is a competitor of mine, what do you do? I handle the grain only at the country point, which is the least paying portion of the handling. How will that affect the grain trade in the west?
Why?

The hon.
member asks me why. I am prepared to discuss it, but frankly I do not want to labour the question before the House. I appreciate the courteous hearing which has been accorded me. I am a new member and diffident about taking up too much time, but this question is of such vital importance to the west that I press it. Without any intention of being discourteous, I would ask hon. gentlemen to make a note of their questions, and when I have finished my argument, to submit them to me, when I will answer them frankly and candidly, so far as I am able.
I want hon. members to follow this and understand it. Those in favour of this legislation will endeavour to impress you-and perhaps they will succeed-with the argument that there is justification for that diversion of the grain from my country elevator and my terminal to their terminal. They feel confident, I have no doubt, that they can
Canada Grain Act

advance reasons for that diversion. As to that I will speak a little later, but at this point I want to bring home to hon. members of this House the fact that my grain handling plant is an economic entity, consisting of terminal capacity and country elevator capacity. My money has been invested in a system of grain handling whereby, in effect, the practice has been for me to gather grain in the country and transmit it to my terminal. That is why I built the terminal and the country elevators. They now ask that a change in the manner of handling that grain be brought about by legislation, with this effect: that every poo! farmer or other farmer who stores grain in my country house can come to me any say: "Kennedy, I want you to send that grain which you have in storage in your country plant, not to your terminal elevator but to the pool terminal." What is the effect? It must be obvious. If hon. members agree-and I know by then . attitude that they have agreed-that the profitable part of my plant is the terminal plant, then every carload of grain which, under ordinary circumstances would be fed to my terminal plant by my country elevator, is diverted from my country elevator to their pool terminal elevators, is a loss of business to my terminal and a gain of business to theirs. I want hon. members to observe that in the handling' of grain the pool is a competitor and a real competitor. Is that proceeding along sound business lines of legislation?
If the private grain trade of the west had a legislative monopoly on the gathering of grain there, well might an organization of farmers such as the pool come to this House and say: You by legislation have given a monopoly of gathering grain in the west to private grain companies. We now demand legislation whereby we can get to our terminal elevators at least that portion of grain which belongs to the farmers who have entered our pool. If that were the situation I would not have the temerity to stand here for one moment to-night to oppose it, but that is not the situation. The grain trade of the west is not controlled by any legislative mono-' poly; it is being handled, as I say, by men who have risked their millions by way of investment in building up the business. They say to you to-night and they say to the pool: We take no issue with your objective to transmit wheat to your pool terminals and keep it in your own hands throughout the whole process of gathering and feeding it to the world markets as you like. But we do take strenuous objection to your asking for legislative powers that will compel us to use

our country plants, not only to gather and store your grain, but having so gathered it, to transmit it, divert it from our terminals to the pool terminals, our competitor, thereby resulting in loss of business to our terminal plants and, by the same token, in gain of business to the terminal plants of our great competitor.	[DOT]
Moreover the effect of this legislation is to compel me as a private grain dealer, not only to divert the grain from my terminal elevator to the pool terminal, but, having parted with the custody of the grain at the country point thousands of miles, it may 'be, from the terminal elevator, to assume absolute responsibility for its safe delivery at the pool terminal on track guaranteeing grade and weight. If there foe leakage en route who suffers the loss? If there be accident en route who suffers the loss? It is up to the private grain dealer to stand that loss without any remuneration. That is the situation. They urge witfi much show of reason this principle. For instance a pool farmer says: "I have Cultivated the soil; I have grown this carload of wheat on my farm; I have gathered it, threshed it, brought it in and stored it in a warehouse belonging to a private company. Why should I not have the right to go to that warehouse and say: Deliver to me my identical property, my grain, in a car here?" They have that power; they can get that identical grain by virtue of provision in the Grain Act with respect to special binning. Of course in the rush season there are not special bins available for all who want them, but at present they have the right to come to my elevator and say: "I want to 'special bin' this," and if there is a bin available, under the law' I must allocate that bin upon request, giving him a warehouse receipt for the weight of grain stored. When he orders his car I put the wheat in his car and I am done with it.
On the other hand if there is not special binning capacity and a Sfarmer comtes to me with a carload of wheat, since no special bin is available the grain must be mixed with other wheat because you cannot keep a separate bin for every farmer. As the wheat must be mixed with other wheat we must first decide what grade that grain is. I examine the grain and say: "I will give you No. 2 northern." Hon. members will remember that I am dealing with men experienced in grading grain. If the farmer is satisfied with that, he says: "All right." I tell him how much the dockage will be and he agrees to that. The only thing that remains to be done is to weigh the grain. I put the grain in a bin with other grain which I have graded

Canada Grain Act
No. 2 northern. Another farmer comes along and the same thing happens, so that very soon in the one bin I may have the grain mixed of half a dozen or a dozen farmers. I shall have No. 1 northern in one bin, No. 2 northern in another, No. 3 northern in another and so on. At once hon. members will see that the identity of that grain is lost. Unlike furniture, the identity of which can be retained in storage, the identity of grain is lost as soon as it is mixed with other grain. But the farmer has a warehouse receipt that shows that I have taken into storage 1,500 bushels of No. 2 northern with a certain dockage. There is the right on which he stands. There is the document on which I must settle.
He has two rights. If he wants to take charge of that grain at the country elevator he orders a car. He comes to me and he says:	"Kennedy, load my grain into car so
and so." I do it. If he takes charge of that car, at once you will observe the practical difficulty arises that is urged by the western grain growers, and I accede to it. I load the farmer's grain in that way and I tell him I have weighed 1,500 bushels of No. 2 northern into that car. He may have a doubt as to the weight in that car; he may have some doubt as to the grade. That car is shipped and it arrives at the terminal fifty or a hundred bushels short. He comes back to me and he says: "Kennedy, my car is fifty or a hundred bushels short," as the case may be. I ask my operator and he says: "I weighed in the full weight." The question arises: Why is it short? Did it leak in transit? That is the question to be decided between the farmer, the railway company and the elevator company and it presents a practical difficulty. So in the trade the practice has developed that instead of the farmer taking delivery at the country point, with the exception of at the outside about five per cent, he takes delivery at the terminal elevator of the company that has his grain in storage at the country points, and the company guarantees his weight and grade, taking all chance of loss in transit by leakage and otherwise. By this legislation he wants the right to take delivery not at my terminal but at the country point and yet have the company guarantee weight and grade at the distant terminal. Why? The reason is obvious; it is because he has en-10 p.m. tered into the grain handling business and he wants to get the grain to feed his terminals. So he says: Give us a law that will make the private company not only deliver the grain at a country point but guarantee the weight and
grade not at the country point of delivery but at the pool terminal at Fort William or wherever it may be.
Now, it may be urged: You took into store 1,500 bushels of his grain, No. 2 Northern; if you load it into his car on the track at the country point he is not there perhaps when it is loaded, and if he is he cannot tell by looking at it its weight nor its grade; therefore why should you not guarantee it at the other end? He has his remedy. Why should I be asked to give up possession of the goods in my storage, turn them over to his custody and let him take them a thousand miles or more on a car that he has ordered from the railway, not I-it may be full of leaks so far as I know-why should I be bound to run all the risk without the custody and guarantee-to him weight and grade at the other end? Suppose he puts this question: Well, if you do not guarantee weight and grade at the other end, how do I know I will get there the weight and grade my certificate admits? This is the way the law now stands, as I have already stated: If the grade remains in my custody and is shipped through my terminal, I give him a terminal warehouse receipt that he can go on the market with and demand delivery from my terminal of the exact quantity of grain that his certificate calls for in weight and grade and dockage. But he says: I do not want to do that, I want this legislation to get around that very thing; I want my grain to go to the pool terminal, not to yours. Well, this is my answer-the same answer that I would give to any other competitor: If you want the grain to go to your terminal, then you do what every other dealer in grain does, you provide the facilities in the country for gathering that grain; and if you build or acquire or lease your own country elevators and gather that grain, you can ship it to Timbuctoo if you wish, or to any other point. That is the answer.
Is that a solution beyond their power? If this law goes through-and a man does not need to be in the trade to know what will	happen-instead	of the terminal
elevators of the private line companies working to capacity, they will be working on part time. I wonder if eastern members realize what the investment in a terminal elevator means? Approximately the cost of a terminal elevator is $1 per bushel of capacity; thus, a terminal of 1,000,000 bushels capacity means $1,000,000 of investment; of 2,000.000 bushels capacity an investment of $2,000,000. Now, I direct this situation to the attention of any hon. mem-

ber or any group of hon. members: Suppose you have $1,000,000 tied up in terminal elevators, just as soon as you begin to divert the grain that feeds those elevators and keeps them busy, so soon you begin to out down on your profit-if you have a profit- until you come to the point where you investment no longer pays a profit, and eventually. you get down to where it is a losing investment. You all know what that comes to. And so the grain trade say to the pool: We recognize you as a big competitor, as a growing competitor, as a serious competitor, but we stake our judgment on this-that it is efficiency which in the long run will get the business, and we are willing to pit our experience, our investment of capital and our method of handling grain against the pool method; we challenge you-if I may use that term-to proceed along the ordinary lines of competition, and we await the result with confidence.
Suppose pool members say, as hon. members who are urging this bill say:	Well, if

ing grain. In addition the western farmers, through the United Grain Growers, own considerable additional country space, and with that held by other private farmers' companies of a smaller nature it may be conservatively stated that the producers themselves own or control from a quarter to a third of the country elevator space for the handling of this year's crop. Therefore, so far as all space is concerned, it will own or control from a quarter to a third of the total space. You must remember, too, that the pool has only been in operation for a short time, and in a period of three years the three principal pools have gone thus far towards solving this economic problem. But where the shoe pinches is that they have signed up about 50 per cent of the grain and want all that grain in their terminal elevators. That is the rub, and we say to them, "Get it there the way any other company would get it".
Now I am going to appeal to the champions of the pool to forget for a moment, if they can, the political expediency of this legislation, and to view it as business men. If they had the money invested, as have the private grain trade how would they view this legislation? Is it to be supported by self-interest alone? Self-interest will dictate that any member of this House who is also a member of the pool will vote for this amendment, which is demanded by the pool. And if they recognize the necessity of catering to the wave of enthusiasm in the west in favour of the pool system of marketing, to which system I take no objection, they cannot help but support the amendment. But I ask them, perhaps without avail, to divorce themselves from immediate self-interest and from political expediency. I say to you that already, under your system of co-operative marketing, you have proceeded far; under propitious circumstances you have met with a large measure of success, from which I have no desire to detract. I congratulate the farmers of western Canada on the success which has attended their efforts through the pool, but having succeeded that far by. the usual means of competition and your own intelligently directed energ3r, I urge upon you to seek not unfair advantage by legislation, in order to bring about a- little faster what you yourselves claim you will do in any event by competition. Pass the word along to your men, if you like; tell the rank and file of the pool that the battle cry is to be, "No quarter to the grain trade
of western Canada". Men of British traditions have heard and given the slogan of "No quarter" before, and they have always accepted it. The grain trade can take no exception to such an ultimatum, but I ask you to pause and consider. Suppose the effect of your legislation should be to eliminate entirely private investment in the grain trade of the west; you will then eliminate, although you may not take it very seriously, a factor from the handling of grain which to my mind goes to the root of the handling of all commodities; I refer to strong competition. If you drive out private competition from the handling of grain in the west and place it in the hands of a monopoly, however ideal it may be in theory, I warn you that you are courting a danger from which you may some day be glad to flee. I say to you then, do not ask this House to legislate your competitors out of business; do not seek to crucify on the cross of political expediency an investment of $85,000,000; do not let us stamp Canada as a country which lightly deals with the rights of invested capital. Hon. members may say to you as they have said to me, "Where did they get the money? If we did wipe it out they would not lose very much, even though $85,000,000 is invested." Some have had the temerity to say, "They got it from us, and if we take it away from them they are not entitled to much sympathy". That is a vicious principle on which to proceed with legislation. The money is there invested in plant and equipment; do not lightly pass legislation that will tend to confiscate it.
In closing I say to this House that Canada needs private capital for its development, not only for the grain trade but for our resources generally. This money that stands to-night invested in the grain trade in the west to the amount of $85,000,000 was invested certainly not with any idea that legislation would be passed that would tend to confiscate it. I urge upon the House therefore to remember that the future of Canada demands this, that private capital shall not have any special privilege, but that it shall have at least such a measure of protection as will not only reasonably safeguard its investment, but will tend to attract to this country capital for its development.

Mr. Chairman, I have no desire to take up much time debating this question because it has been fairly well threshed out in the committee on Agriculture and aroupd the corridors. I believe most members are fairly familiar with the case for both sides. However, in view of the statements put before the House to-night, I feel that there is an obligation on me to present
Canada Grain Act

the case from our side, and in opening perhaps I might give a brief history of the pool, what it is, and what it stands for.
The first pool operating in western Canada was that organized in the province of Alberta, which began its operations in 1923 and handled the crop for that year. The pools organized in Saskatchewan and Manitoba operated first in 1924. The three pools last year handled 81,500,000 bushels of wheat, besides a considerable quantity of other grains. This year it is estimated that the joint pools will handle at least 200,000,000 bushels of wheat, besides a very considerable quantity of coarse grains.
Some estimate of the importance of the pool and of the volume of its business may be gathered from the fact that next year's business will probably more than double the annual gross earnings of the Canadian Pacific Railway. In one interim payment made by the pool in March last, the amount of S37,000,000 was paid out in one day to the farmers. That was one of four payments. The pool now has offices at Vancouver, Calgary, Regina, Winnipeg, Fort William, Toronto, New York and Paris, and has made connections with agencies in every important country in the world. The pool will have in Alberta this fall for the handling of grain 33 of its own elevators, and will also have a joint control in the operation of 1S6 others, or a total of 219 elevators. In Saskatchewan they will have 571 elevators, and in Manitoba by next fall they will be operating 40. This makes a total of 830 elevators, which is 20 per cent of the total of 4,300 elevators in western Canada. The total terminal capacity at the head of the lakes is
64,700,000	bushels. Of this the pool at the present time controls 17,450,000 bushels, or 27 per cent of the total. The total capacity of the 4,300 country elevators in the prairie provinces is 143,351,000 bushels.
All this controversy arose, I may say, over section 159, which was the original section in the 1912 Canada Grain Act. As we understood that section, it did give to the farmer the right to determine the destination of his grain, and I do not know of a single instance in the last twenty-five years where a farmer putting his grain in a special bin in a country elevator was ever refused the right to ship that grain to any terminal of his choice. There are many farmers in this House to-night on both sides who have exercised this privilege for the last twenty or twenty-five -years, and to whom it has never been denied.
We have two farmer elevator companies operating in western Canada-the Saskatchewan Co-operative, and the United Crain

Growers. In my own district many a shareholder in one of those companies has found that his own elevator was plugged, and that he could not take his grain in there, but he was able to secure a bin in one of the line elevators, and was always permitted to have his grain shipped from that elevator direct to the terminal elevator of his own company. I do not know of a single instance in which he was ever denied that right. The elevator companies naturally must have assumed that the law compelled them to do that, or they would not have carried it out.
The particular clause which deals with this phase of the situation was, however, rather ambiguous because it says, as anyone may see who will look at section 159, "if either party so desires." That is in reference to shipping grain to the terminal of his choice. That being somewhat ambiguous, Chief Justice Turgeon, with the consent and approval of the Board of Grain Commissioners in drafting the new clause introduced in the bill of last year made it read, "if he so desires." He put it beyond all doubt that the right was in the hands of the farmer, and the farmer only, to determine the destination of his grain. That, I may say, was the clause in bill No. 113 of last year, the bill which had its first reading in this House on May 11, 1925. In the Agriculture committee last year, however, the grain interests were able to secure the passage of an amendment which took away from the farmer that right by altering the wording of this clause, and in addition, not being satisfied with that, they added another clause, which distinctly and specifically relieved the country elevator from all responsibility for weight and grade in case the farmer exercised this right.
The argument is used-I think it was used by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre to-night-that the farmer still has the right to determine the destination of his grain under the present act. Technically that is so; in reality it is not so, because under this disability, with the country elevator relieved of responsibility for the weight and grade, the farmer cannot possibly exercise that right. I do not suppose there was a single instance in western Canada last year where the farmer would take that chance.
In dealing with the situation as regards the country elevator, I may say that the transportation is part of the system. The country elevator is not a private institution. It is a semi-public institution. It has a public duty to perform. It is licensed1 by a public body, and recognized by law, and given certain rights and privileges, and placed under cer-

Canada Grain Act
tain restrictions. Being given those rights, it has certain public duties to perform, and part of those duties in the handling of special bin grain is to guarantee the weight and grade at the other end; that is, when a farmer secures a special bin in a country elevator and has a carload of grain put in there, when it is loaded out on the car on the track the responsibility of the elevator has not ceased. The system and the law has always recognized that the farmer, not being in a position to check the weight and the grade in the car, must be guaranteed that weight and that grade when it is delivered at the terminal elevator. I might add that the handling charges are based on that. The elevator companies have staffs of men at Winnipeg who examine these cars las soon as they arrive there. They are notified by the railway company, and they examine the cars to see that there is no leakage or damage to the car itself, and they check the grade and the weight. They have a similar staff at the terminal points, at Port Arthur and Fort William, and at other points to which the grain may be shipped. This, I may say, is included in the handling charges. That is the elevator company are supposed to be paid a sufficient sum to reimburse them for the cost of examining these cars.
What is the charge?

The regular charge for special bin grain is 1J cents per bushel, but they are permitted by the Board of Grain Commissioners to charge 2i cents per bushel. I may say that except in very rare instances they do not exercise that right. They prefer to handle it at If cents a bushel which is the prevailing rate charg<?d in western Canada.
What do the country elevators get now, under the law, for handling grain?
Under the law the elevators are permitted to charge 2J cents per bushel.
That is for special bin grain?
Yes.
And for grain other than special bin grain lj cents?
Yes.'

If this bill passes you will be allowed to have the grain diverted from the country elevator direct to
your pool terminal. With the private company guaranteeing wheat to the pool terminal, is there not an additional charge provided for under the proposed amendment?
The present regulations provide for a charge of 2| cents a bushel, as I said, but the elevator companies do not exercise that right.

I am not
talking about special bin grain but grain stored in country elevators. If this bill passes will they not be entitled to charge lj cents for handling grain at country points?

In the first place, there being no extra responsibility, it is not necessary for them to make any extra charge. The Canada Grain Act, I may explain for the benefit of the hon. gentleman, does not set the charges; it authorizes the Board of Grain Commissioners to set charges that in their estimation will be fair. The Board of Grain Commissioners meet every year for the purpose of discussing this question with the grain trade and setting what they consider a maximum charge. If they find, after a few years, that the elevators cannot be made to pay we have authority to say-and I say here tonight on the authority of the board- there is no question whatever but that the board will raise the rate in order to permit the operations of the elevators to pay.

Another
question-
I think the hon. member should be fair. He asked me not to interrupt him while he was speaking.

As you gave me a most attentive hearing I was going to ask you whether you would prefer that I should ask you these questions as the points arise, or reserve them until you are through. If it is your wish that I should reserve the questions until you are through, I shall gladly do so.

I think I would prefer to take the hon. gentleman at his own word. He appealed to myself and others not to interrupt him while he was speaking. I am quite ready to accord to him the same courtesy he accorded to us; I am quite ready to answer any of his questions at the close of my speech.
I may say there are two classes of grain. These are subdivided into other classes but for the sake of argument I will say there are simply two. The first class is street grain and the second is special bin grain. Street grain
Canada Grain Act

is the grain that comes in by wagon load; that is where the farmer cannot make up a car and he simply sells his grain by the wagon load direct to the elevator company. Special bin grain is grain that the farmer does not want to sell at that particular time. He simply uses the elevator company for warehousing purposes. He secures a special bin, has his grain placed in that bin, and has it shipped out to his order to whatever elevator he chooses.
Dealing now with the question of weights and grades out of the country elevator, I may say that the farmer authorizes the elevator man to order the car when he wants that grain shipped out. The farmer is out on his farm five, ten, perhaps fifteen or twenty miles from town in a good many cases. He may be in a place where -there is no telephone, and he has no idea when the car will arrive. Sometimes the farmers have to wait months, actually months, before they can secure the necessary cars. As occasionally happens a trainload of cars will arrive late in the evening in a small town and the grain will be lo-aded in-to them by the elevator. In the busy season the elevator man will go to work at night to load that grain out; the farmer has no means of knowing when that is done. The first thing he knows about it, perhaps, is when these cars are hundreds of miles away on the road to the Great -Lakes. Therefore the argument that the farmer can be on hand to see his grain loaded into -the car is absolutely absurd. Any practical farmer in the House knows that it cannot be done except in very rare instances-in fact I will go further and say that I -think in the majority of cases the grain is not weighed at all. When his grain is put into special bins the elevator -man gives him a ticket for so many bushels. In many cases when that grain is loaded i-t is shot direct from the bin into the car; it is not put through the scales -at all. The elevator .man will -report to his company not the exact weight but what the storage tickets call for. We do not assume that these elevator men are all dishonest, although in many cases they are. The police court records of western Canada will show a great many cases where these elevator men have been dishonest. However, that is not our reason for objecting to their weight. It is very easy for the most honest man to -make a mistake. The farmers bring their wheat to the elevator in wagons. I have seen ten, fifteen, and twenty teams lined up behind each other waiting to unload into the elevator. Farmer No. 1 has a certain bin. He asks that

his grain be loaded in that bin. The elevator man starts his engine and the grain is elevated into tha-t particular bin. T-he very moment the first farmer's team pulls out another man comes in who has another bin. The elevator man then switches his spout to another position and it is very easy sometimes for him to get grain mixed. Any elevator man will tell you that one hundred or three hundred bushels of one man's grain may very easily get into another -bin. When a particular car is loaded it is sealed up and shipped out. WTe will say in this particular case the farmer exercises the technical right which the act gives him of shipping to the pool terminal. But when the car gets there it is found that it is 100 bushels short. The a-ct distinctly states that the elevator company shall not be responsible for that weight. Who does the weighing? The weighing in to the terminal elevator is done by government weighmasters who have no monetary interest in the grain there and whose scales are checked up repeatedly. Their scales are inspected and representatives of the elevator company stand by the scales and see every pound of their own grain weighed. Therefore I say the farmer has a perfect right to refuse to accept the weights set -by the country elevator. But what does the elevator company do? They refuse to accept the government weights. In effect they state that they have not confidence in the government weighmaster, and -they tell you that they have no right to examine these cars or to check weights and grades. That is another argument that cannot be backed up. When a farmer exercises his right to have a car of grain shipped to a pool- terminal the elevator company cannot -govern that but it can endorse on the bill of lading we will say for instance, "Advise the Pioneer Grain -Company, Winnipeg". When a car of grain so billed arrives at Winnipeg, notwithstanding the fact that it is pool grain and that it was shipped by a farmer through a -line elevator, that elevator company is immediately notified by the railway company. They have a staff for that purpose and they can go and examine the car. If there should be a broken seal, if there should be any sign of leakage, they immediately report it to the railway company and -they have a claim for damages against the company if it does not weigh out at the terminal elevator. When it -arrives at the terminal they have the same opportunity to check it. They are in identically the same position as they would be if the grain were going to their own elevator, and I defy the hon. member from Winnipeg South Centre, or

anyone speaking from the viewpoint of the grain exchange to-day, to show me any material difference between the case of a car shipped direct to their own terminal, and the case of a car billed as I have suggested, going to the pool terminal, where they have a terminal of their own.

I accept
that challenge.

All right. The question arises, why does the farmer want to determine the destination of his grain? There are various reasons, and I will not give them in detail. I will give a specific instance to illustrate one of the reasons why the farmer wants his grain to go to his own terminal. I am speaking now of course from the standpoint of the pool, but before I am through I propose to speak from the standpoint of the non-pool farmer, because we are fighting the battle of the non-pool farmer just as much as the battle of the pool farmer. A farmer residing in a part of my constituency last year had two fields of wheat, one grown on summer fallow and the other on spring plowing. When he sent his samples to Winnipeg they were each graded No. 2. Under our grading system they graded exactly the same, but the grain grown on the summer fallow had a much higher protein content, which made it more valuable for milling purposes than the car of grain grown on spring plowing, although the grade was identically the same as the other. The farmer sent samples to a grain company in Minneapolis. One of them they passed on as a straight grade, and they would not pay more than the market price for it. On the other they offered a premium of 26 cents a bushel, because it was very much more valuable for milling ' purposes; the higher-priced would have netted the farmer nearly $400 per car. That is one of the reasons-I do not say the only one-why we want our grain to go to our own terminals, or why the farmer wants to determine the terminals to which his grain shall be sent, and also the reason why the grain companies want to have all the grain sent to their own terminals, whether the farmer wants it or not. We are not denying to the grain companies the right to send their own grain to their own terminals. They have a perfect right to do it and to get all the premiums they can on their own grain. But we object to giving them the privilege -it is not a right-of sending grain that does not belong to them to their own terminals, selling some of it as premium grain, securing the premium price for it, and delivering to the pool terminals grain of a similar grade,
but of a quality that does not command the premium. That is one of the reasons why we want our grain to go to our own terminal and one of the reasons why they want to ship it direct to their terminals.
The argument has been frequently used that the country elevator system and the terminal elevator are a unit, and that if you separate them you destroy the system. The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre stated that first a company builds a line of country elevators; that then they must of necessity build a terminal to handle the grain at the other end, and that if we use country elevators and ship the grain to whatever elevator we like, we are simply destroying the system. On the face of it I will admit that it looks plausible, but when you examine into it you will find there is nothing in it at all. I ask the member for Winnipeg South Centre, if that be so, how do the government terminals exist at all? Because the government own a tremendous amount of terminal space and have not one single country elevator, and it is only in so far as we depart from the present law that the government elevators are able to get any grain at all. The law to-day actually prevents grain going to government elevators. It is a direct discrimination against them, and I may say for the benefit of the hon. member and those who agree with him that a considerable number of grain companies operating elevators in the prairies to-day do not own terminals a tall. One such company is operating in my constituency, and so far as I know they make good profits and earn good dividends. One of the largest companies in western Canada, the one that showed the highest profits, was the Alberta Pacific Company. They have shown substantial profits, although they never owned any terminal elevator.
The question is asked, if the pool grain is passed through the country elevator and then all of it is permitted to go to the pool terminals, what are they going to do with the other terminal elevators? What is going to be done with them? I may say at the outset that there is not a bushel of terminal storage at the head of the lakes more than we need in a year when there is a good crop. That is proved by the fact that last year the pool in the 'busy season had to divert 5,000 cars of its own grain which it was not able to take care of itself, to outside elevators. Take an extreme case: suppose that all the local elevators of a certain company were used for pool grain, and not one bushel of grain was permitted to go to their own terminals- of course such condition is impossible but
Canada Grain Act

we will take it as an hypothetical case-it would simply mean that the other terminal elevators could not accommodate that grain, and that particular terminal elevator would have to be used, either purchased or leased in some way. We all realize that in such a case we are up against economic laws. The men operating the pool are sensiblte business men, and they know that if they go to the terminal elevator and offer either to buy or lease, they must pay the value. If they buy it, they must pay the replacement value, and if they lease it they must pay sufficient to provide a good dividend on the money invested and all operating charges. They would have to do it if they built it themselves. There is no desire on their part to confiscate anything, nor could they do it.
The.hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre tried to make a strong point of vested rights. He told us that there was invested in the . grain handling facilities in western Canada about 185,000,000, and that this investment was going to be seriously jeopardized if the amendment went through. A good deal of this investment is government money. They have a very large proportion of it. In addition to that, the pool itself has about a third of the investment. Well, perhaps I am not correct in saying a third. The poo! has about a third of the terminal storage and a smaller proportion of the country elevators, but at any rate, deducting the government investment, deducting the pool's investment, deducting the investment of another farmer's company, the United Grain Growers, I think I am safe in saying that the interests that are fighting this amendment to-day have an investment of not more than 145,000,000. On the other hand, what has the farmer got? According to last Canada Year Book the farmers of Western Canada have an investment of $3,350,000,000, or eighty times as much as the grain trade. My hon. friend will raise his hands in holy horror at the idea of jeopardizing an investment of $45,000,000, but if the amendment does not go through we are injuring vested rights eighty times as great. The secretary of the Grain Exchange, addressing the Agriculture committee, stated quite frankly that the pool could put the grain men out of business in two years. His exact words were that they could put them out of business in two years anyway. Supposing that to be so, supposing that in two years' time most of these grain companies go out of business, what will be the position of the non-pool farmers? because there will always be non-pool farmers. I am a strong supporter of the pool myself; my grain goes [Mr. Campbell. 1
through it; I believe in supporting it, and I do not think I shall have any reason to change my mind. But I am not so optimistic as to believe that the day will ever come when every bushel of grain in western Canada will go through the pool, I think there will always be a grain exchange and always non-pool farmers. I ask hon. gentlemen then to consider seriously the position of these companies operating on the grain exchange and the position of nonpool farmers if this amendment does not go through. I am really arguing from the standpoint of my hon. friend, only I am looking ahead a couple of years. I am quite prepared to make the prediction now that if this amendment does not go through, within two years you will find officials of the grain exchange and these lawyers who are representing them here to-day coming to Ottawa and pleading with tears in their eyes to put through, in the interest of the grain companies and the non-pool farmers, the very amendment they are asking you to reject to-day. There is no question about that.
In my constituency there are a number of sidings where this year there will be none but pool elevators. That means that nonpool farmers at those particular points will have no other means of shipping their grain except over the platform, and it is only practicable to use that at certain times. The law as it stands to-day would at these points give the pool elevator a distinct advantage. Suppose a farmer thinks he has premium grain. He wants to take advantage of that fact. He puts it into a special bin in the pool elevator; he instructs the pool to ship it; but the pool exercises its right under this act- there is no reason why it should not-and ships it to its own terminal. If it is premium grain the pool will secure the premium and it will go into the pool for the benefit of the pool farmers. The farmer, the owner of the grain, will have delivered to some grain company to whom he wishes to sell his grain, grain of a similar grade, but the stuff is not premium grain. There is no question about that. The men who are operating the pool elevators are shrewd business men; they will not let an opportunity like that pass, and since the grain companies take advantage of the present law, most assuredly the pool elevators will take advantage of it themselves. What is then the position of the non-pool farmer? What is the position of the independent grain company operating on the grain exchange? There may be some of them who want to buy grain at points where there are none but pool elevators. They may buy grain through the country merchant or dealers

Canada Grain Act
working on commission, but the law distinctly prevents them from procuring it-a distinct discrimination. I think I am safe in predicting, as I said before, that if this amendment does not pass now, within two years you will see this same host of gentlemen who are in the corridors to-day, pleading with tears in their eyes for us to pass this very amendment in the interest of the grain exchange and the non-pool farmers.
I	want to make it distinctly understood that while we may be primarily representing the pool, we are pleading for a cause that is really in the interest of all the farmers and will eventually be in the interest of the grain trade itself. How does it happen to-day that we find the grain trade lined up on one side and the pool on the other? It is simply a coincidence, because it happens that the pool have about 50 or 60 per cent of the grain, but only a small proportion, about 20 per cent, of the country elevators. So the injustice in the aggregate is done to the pool. But in two years, according to Dr. Magill's prediction, the situation will be reversed and there is no doubt that the pool will have 80 per cent of the elevators and 80 per cent or more of the grain. Then what will be the position of the farmers who own the other 20 per cent of the grain, and what opportunity will the man operating on the grain exchange have-because I think there will still be a grain exchange-to secure that grain in its purity directly from the farmer?
The question of rates, of course, has figured very largely in this debate. The grain men tell us that if the country elevators are taken away from them; that is, if we are allowed to use the country elevators for storage purposes only, they will lose a great deal of money because the country elevators do not pay. I am not certain whether that is true
or not, but I am not going to
II p.m. argue the point. To me it is
immaterial whether they pay or not. But if they do not pay the fault is with the elevator companies themselves because they are permitted for " special bin " grain to charge 2% cents per bushel, but they charge only 1J cents. It is true that on the other stored grain they are permitted to charge only 1| cents, but we have it on the word of the Board of Grain Commisisoners that if necessary they will be permitted to charge higher rates and we know they must be so permitted if they cannot be operated at a profit at present rates. The question arises why they do not exercise the right they have to-day to charge higher rates than they are now charging. The whole situation is this,
that if the local elevator paid very well many country merchants, many groups of farmers, would go in and build elevators themselves. That is a condition the grain trade do not want; so by operating their country elevators at a loss they are able to secure a complete monopoly of the receiving end, and they can easily make up at the terminal what they lose at the country point. That is the situation. They are not frank and honest with us to-day in stating the situation as it is.
They also use the argument that if they charge higher rate the farmers will load their grain over the loading plaform. There may be in western Canada points where the farmers have gone fairly extensively into mixed farming, where grain is only a portion of the total products, where perhaps they could, with facility, handle there a little bit of grain over the platform. But that is not so in the great majority of cases in western Canada. In my town we have five elevators and the car loading platform has accommodation for only two cars. It will take the average farmer from two to four days to load a car. With the quantity of grain shipped out of that point, even if they started loading on the first January and continued loading until the end of December of the same year, they could not load the total crop over the platform, and the amount the farmer would pay in demurrage charges would often be more than he would pay in elevator charges. Therefore that argument does not hold good, and if the elevator companies want to make the local elevators pay all they have to do is to ask for higher rates and be prepared to deal with competition at the country end.
There is one argument that our friends of the grain exchange have used around1 the corridors and in some of the committee rooms, but they have not used it before the Agricultural committee, nor publicly. It is this: They say that the pool to-day has an elevator at Buffalo and that if this amendment goes through and permits the pool to ship to their own terminal, it will assist in the diversion of Canadian grain to United States ports. What are the facts? In the first place the pool, I may say, did not build a terminal at Buffalo; they took over the Saskatchewan Co-operative Company's elevators and1 this terminal was included. But as the situation stands to-day at the Canadian ports of Quebec, St. John, Halifax and other points like that there are no elevators except government elevators, and as the law now stands it puts an impediment in the way of grain movement through those ports. Indeed it is only through the operations of the pool and of the law as
Canada Grain Act

we expect to have it after this amendment passes that grain can go forward to those ports. The figures prove that every bushel shipped to the port of Quebec last year was pool grain. It would not be company grain because they send their grain to their own terminals and they have no elevators at Quebec, St. John or Halifax. If hon. mem-ers will look up the prices, they will find that prices of grain futures on the grain exchange are for delivery at the head of the lakes only. A miller in England buys a certain quantity of grain for delivery in May, July, October and so on. The price on futures on the Winnipeg Exchange is quoted to him f.oJb. head of the lakes, and the head of the lakes only. He cannot secure a future price on St. John, Halifax or Quebec. Why? Because through the operations of the grain exchange these Canadian ports are discriminated against. There is no question about it. Let me ask you: Who all these years has been fighting for the retention of our grain by our own ports; who in this House for the last four years has been fighting for it? The farmer group in this section of the House, joined recently by another farmer group in another part of the House. One of the reasons why we want to retain the grain in our own ports is because we wish it to go to the old country in its purity. We know that in transit through the United States it has been debased in grade; we know that while it has borne the Canadian grade certificate the Americans have been taking off some of our better grain and substituting their poorer grain therefor, using our better grain for milling purposes and debasing the grade of our grain on the European market. Therefore the pool that we are representing will find it to its interest entirely to divert every bushel of grain it possibly can to Canadian ports.
And what about the elevator at Buffalo? Will all the grain received there go down through American ports? Not at all. The pool has that listed as a transfer house. Through the operation of the Canadian coastal laws, it is often more profitable to ship grain to Buffalo and then tranship it to Montreal than to send it direct to Montreal from the head of the lakes. That is the situation, because American ships can handle the grain on that route but are prevented from doing so on the direct route, and so they cut the rates under all Canadian routes. Consequently a great deal of our grain goes to Buffalo for transhipment to Montreal and it does not go to the ocean through American ports aJt all. That is why the pool lists this elevator as a transfer

house, and as far as I know it will not under ordinary circumstances send one bushel out through United States ports that can possibly be avoided.
Mr. Chairman

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Let me say to the
committee before there is any further discussion that we are on section 1 of Bill No. 8-contents of warehouse receipts. Of course, I understand I have to allow some latitude on the discussion of this clause, but I would ask hon. members to keep as close to the clause as they possibly can.

I think, Mr. Chairman, the matters that have been discussed by both the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) and myself are all very definitely related to just that clause. Now, the hon. member has suggested two or three points and asked two or three questions to which I wish to refer. He states that the country elevators are semi-public institutions, and arguing therefrom he contends that therefore they should be available for whatever purpose the producer of grain desires. The hon. member also says that the country elevators are licensed and regulated by the government. That is true. So is a drug store, so is practically every institution in this country that does business with the public. But because they are so licensed and regulated, does it follow that they are public institutions, to be used by the public for whatever purpose they wish?

May I be permitted
to correct the hon. gentleman?

They represent private investment of capital that is regulated under the terms of the (Grain Act. The hon. gentleman also says he is not sure whether the amount these country elevators are now by law entitled to charge for the handling of grain is remunerative. Now, generally he was very fair, but I think he overstepped the mark a little there. He tells us that our country elevators are entitled to charge 2-1 cents for specially binned grain. That is true. I ask him what percentage of the grain handled in the west is specially binned; is it 10 per cent, taking the whole of the west?
Yes, considerably more.

Would the
hon. member say 15 per cent?

Yes.

It is 50 per cent sometimes

At a given

It depends on the season.

That is
begging the question. I say, averaging the wheat crop year in and year out, not 15 per cent is specially binned.
You are wrong.

Then it is
an honest mistake. That is my definite information. So much for the amount of grain on which they can charge that 2\ cents a bushel for handling. On all the other grain the rate fixed by the Canada grain commissioners is 1J cents a bushel. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggests to this House that he does not know whether or not this rate pays the country elevators. Well, if he does not know, he is the only member of the pool who is in that position. If he refers to the report of the Turgeon Commission, a commission that made a most exhaustive examination of the grain trade generally, he will there find it stated, and it is well known throughout the west by farmers and men in the grain trade, that the 11 cents per bushel handling charge does not pay for the money invested in those country elevators.
The time was when they did pay. They do not pay now because their number has been unduly multiplied by the grain trade.
The hon. member admits that that rate does not pay at the present time?
No.
I am speaking to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar). He has just interpolated that the time was when they did pay, but now they do not.
I admit frankly they do not pay now. They did pay. The reason they do not pay now is that they have been unduly multiplied by the grain trade.

I thank the hon. member for that frank answer-which I could not get from the hon. member who represents Mackenzie-because the hon. member for Qu'Appelle has sat on several grain commissions and knows what he is talking about in that regard. Now the hon. member for Mackenzie says: Well, I have the word of the chairman of the grain commission that if this grain is diverted from the country elevators to our terminals, and if the rate of 11 cents does not pay, then he will regulate it so it will pay. Is that evidence upon which this House should act in view of the admission of the hon. member for Qu'Appelle that 11 cents a bushel handling charge does not pay those private companies? There is no provision in this amendment for increases in rates. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggests that if after 'three or four years' trial we find it does not pay, we have the word of the grain commission that they will raise the rate.
Does not the hon. member know that only a few years ago they offered to handle the grain for nothing? How did they make their money then?
I do not know that as a matter of fact.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to
a question of privilege. The hon. member is misquoting me. He stated that I said if after three or four years we find it does not pay we will raise the rate. I made no such statement whatever.

I accept that; I did not intentionally misquote the hon. member. Cut out the three or four years; what guarantee has this House that if this amendment is passed and it is found that these rates do not pay, they will be raised? I submit that this is not a sufficient ground on which to pass this legislation. The hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) suggests that the elevator companies are willing to accept a lower rate, or to handle it for nothing. I am so accustomed to extreme statements from the hon. member for Rosetown on any subject he discusses that I attach no importance to that remark. The hon. member for Mackenzie says assuming that the private elevator companies do go to the grain commission and say, "One and three-quarters cents handling charge in the country does not pay; we want to raise it to three cents," they will raise it. Suppose it is raised to three cents. In theory that is all right, but what will happen? Take a country point where there is a pool elevator and a private elevator; the private elevator raises its rates to three cents and the pool elevator stores grain for two or two and a
Canada Grain Act

half cents. How much grain will the private elevator get? You may ask how the pool can store it for two or two and a half cents while the other elevator charges three cents. The pool does not need to care; if it loses on storage charges at the country point under the co-operative system those losses will be made up at the other end. So far as the operation of its business goes the pool need not charge a cent at a country point; they could store the grain free. But they would have to make up the loss at the other end, and in the final result it would make no difference to the farmer. Therefore, as a matter of practical competition, the line elevators cannot raise their rates as against the pool elevators.
Carried.

It is not
carried, I may say that since I have been in this House many hours and even days have been spent wrangling over matters of far less importance than this amendment. The hon. member for Mackenzie suggested that it is impossible for the farmer to be present at the country point when his grain is loaded. It is not physically impossible, but I will grant that as a fracti'cal proposition it certainly is not convenient, and if he wishes to term it impossible I will not quarrel with him. But as the law exists the farmer does not need to be present to see his grain weighed, because he has a warehouse receipt which calls for delivery of weight and] grade at the terminal of the company which accepted his grain for storage. The hon. member suggests to this House that if this amendment goes through, private line companies will still have custody of the grain from the time it leaves their country elevator; by some regulation which he suggests but which is not in the act, they are able to keep control' of and examine the grain at any point, and he challenges anyone to deny it. Any man familiar with the shipping of commodities knows that to be impractical and impossible. As soon as the farmer goes to the country elevator and says, "Load out my car of grain and ship it to the pool", what happens? The elevator operator must load that car of grain and bill it, not to his company at the pool but to that farmer at the pool, and at no point in transit has he the right of inspection or examination. I grant you that the hon, member might be able to work out some provision, to go along with this amendment, which would give him that right, but there is nothing of that kind contained in the act and we must take the act as it is.

The hon. member also suggests that they want their own identical grain delivered to the pool in order that they may get the benefit of any additional protein content of any particular wheat. I submit that that is an argument in favour of their objective. I do not dispute it, but let them build their own country elevators, gather the grain afid ship it, and in that way they will get the additional protein content. In querying the position I take as to the economic entity of a company's plant for handling grain, the hon. member suggested that terminal elevators and country elevators were not bound up as an economic entity. He said, "Will the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre tell me how it is that the government's terminal elevators get on without country elevators?" Well, government institutions have a way of getting on without paying their expenses which does not apply to private institutions, and I tell him that the government terminals do not pay as such.

Does the hon. member know that the total earnings of the government elevator at Port Arthur over a period of ten years have been $4024,000 with an expenditure of $'1,474,000, leaving a net operating surplus of $3,450,000?
Let me ask the hon. member a question. Did they make that profit without handling grain?
They made the profit without having any feeder.

Will you
tell me where the private line companies will get their grain, without country feeders?
I suppose they will get it where the government elevators get their grain.

Not if the pool carries out the intention which is suggested as a reason for this amendment. They say they want to get the wheat into their own terminals, and certainly the private line . companies want the same thing. Where the government elevators will get their wheat it is difficult to say unless it is the surplus in busy seasons, and elevators cannot be made to pay on that basis.
Issue has been taken with my statement of the amount of money invested by the private grain trade in elevators, terminals and equipment. My figure of $85,000,000 did not include the pool investment, nor that of the private farmers' companies. This figure was

After my long experience in western Canada, and in the grain business for a very long time, I trust that the committee will bear with me for just a few minutes. I agree that it is well that information should be furnished on the resolution, but I think far too much time of the House has been taken up, certainly this session, in discussing resolutions. The resolution is merely an introductory feature, but in some cases we have spent much more time in discussing the resolution than in discussing the bill itself. At the time the Grand Trunk acquisition took place, the government of the day, which had charge of that measure, refused to allow the resolution even to be discussed, holding it was not debatable. I cite that case to show how much beyond the former point of view the present administration has gone in regard to resolutions which have been introduced.
A departure from sound practice.

I hope the business of the House will not be carried on according to precedents established by former governments. I think it would be far better to give the members of the House some information on the resolution; then if that information leads them to believe the bill should not be introduced, they have a chance to express their opinions. After the bill is introduced and we vote against the second reading, it becomes equivalent to a vote of want of confidence. Therefore I believe the purpose to be servedl by resolutions is altogether lost :if no information be given when the resolution is introduced.
Can the minister give us the total amount loaned up to the present time to the Harbour Commissioners of Montreal?
The amount was $44,000,000 up to December 1 last, upon which they have always paid interest.
How much of principal has been paid?
None at present.

What sinking fund has been provided? It is a very nice thing to
